lesson:
# From algorithm to RTL: the HLS flow

High-level synthesis (HLS) compiles an untimed algorithm, usually C or C++, into a register-transfer-level design: a datapath of functional units, registers and multiplexers, and a controller that sequences it. It sits one level above logic synthesis, and its output is the RTL that Yosys or a commercial tool then maps to gates. A tool designer cares because HLS makes the decisions RTL designers otherwise make by hand: which cycle each operation runs in and which hardware it shares.

## What HLS turns into what

The input is a function whose semantics are sequential and untimed: statements, loops, arrays, arithmetic. The output is a clocked machine that computes the same function. Everything the source states, the arithmetic and the data dependences, is preserved; what the source leaves open is time and space. HLS chooses the clock cycle of every operation (scheduling), how many adders and multipliers exist (allocation), which operation runs on which unit and which register holds which value (binding), and how the block talks to the outside world (interface synthesis). The same C can therefore produce a one-multiplier design that takes 64 cycles or a 64-multiplier design that takes one, depending on directives such as unroll and pipeline. That freedom is the whole point, and also why the result must be verified against the C.

## The steps of the flow

A front end parses the C into an intermediate representation, typically SSA inside a control-data-flow graph, and runs compiler optimizations: inlining, constant propagation, dead-code removal, bit-width narrowing, loop transformations. Then the synthesis core runs. Allocation picks the number of units of each type. Scheduling assigns each operation a control step, respecting dependences and the allocation. Binding maps operations to unit instances and values to registers, which fixes the multiplexers in front of each unit. Finally the tool emits RTL: the datapath, a finite-state machine whose states are the control steps, and the interface logic. A value produced in step 2 and consumed in step 5 must survive two clock edges, so scheduling directly creates register demand. The order matters: binding needs a schedule, and resource-constrained scheduling needs an allocation.

## Where HLS fits and where it struggles

HLS shines on algorithmic blocks with regular loops over arrays: filters, transforms, linear algebra, image pipelines, network packet processing. It struggles where the cycle behavior is the specification, as in a bus protocol defined by a timing diagram, and where hardware cannot be statically sized, as in unbounded recursion or malloc. Its reports of latency, initiation interval and resources are estimates from its own operator models, made before logic synthesis and routing, so the final clock frequency can differ. And because the tool changed the timing, the generated RTL must be checked with C/RTL co-simulation, running the C testbench against the RTL. The practical result is a short design loop: change a directive, re-run HLS in minutes, and compare quality of results, a loop that later invites automation.

## Going deeper

Coussy and Morawiec (eds.), "High-Level Synthesis: From Algorithm to Digital Circuit" (2008); De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapters 4 to 6; Kastner, Matai and Neuendorffer, "Parallel Programming for FPGAs" (2018).

Compared with logic synthesis, what is the main new decision that HLS makes?

A) Time: it schedules operations into clock cycles and shares hardware across cycles

B) Retiming registers across existing combinational logic

C) Two-level minimization of each output

D) Technology mapping of Boolean functions onto library cells
problems.a: Time: it schedules operations into clock cycles and shares hardware across cycles
problems.e: Logic synthesis starts from RTL whose cycle behavior is fixed. HLS chooses that cycle behavior, then reuses units over time.

A) A gate-level netlist mapped to a standard-cell library

B) A placed and routed layout of the function

C) An RTL datapath of functional units, registers and multiplexers, plus an FSM controller that sequences it

D) A binary that runs on an embedded processor
problems.a: An RTL datapath of functional units, registers and multiplexers, plus an FSM controller that sequences it
problems.e: HLS stops at register-transfer level: a datapath and its controller. Logic synthesis and physical design take it from there.

A) Allocation

B) Functional-unit binding

C) Chaining

D) Register binding

problems.e: Allocation chooses the number and type of units; scheduling and binding then work within it.

After scheduling, a value is produced in step 2 and consumed in step 5. What hardware does that imply?

A) A register that holds the value across the step boundaries

B) A latch clocked on the opposite edge

C) A FIFO between two clock domains

D) A plain wire with no storage
problems.a: A register that holds the value across the step boundaries
problems.e: A value that crosses a clock edge must be stored. Register binding later decides which register holds it.

A) Interface synthesis

B) Allocation

C) Scheduling

D) Functional-unit binding
problems.a: Functional-unit binding
problems.e: Allocation fixes how many multipliers exist; binding decides which operation runs on which one.

A C function uses recursion of data-dependent depth and malloc. What will a typical HLS tool do?

A) Synthesize one level of the recursion and ignore the rest

B) Reject it or require a rewrite, because hardware needs statically bounded storage and call depth

C) Move the function onto a soft processor automatically

D) Synthesize a hardware stack of unbounded size
problems.a: Reject it or require a rewrite, because hardware needs statically bounded storage and call depth
problems.e: Every register and memory in hardware has a fixed size, so the synthesizable subset of C excludes unbounded recursion and dynamic allocation.

D) Move the function onto a soft processor automatically
problems.a: Reject it or require a rewrite, because hardware needs statically bounded storage and call depth
problems.e: Every register and memory in hardware has a fixed size, so the synthesizable subset of C excludes unbounded recursion and dynamic allocation.

problems.q:
Why do teams verify HLS output with C/RTL co-simulation instead of trusting the C test alone?

A) C compilers cannot run testbenches

B) RTL simulators run faster than compiled C

C) HLS tools always change the arithmetic results

D) The generated RTL adds timing and interface behavior that the C model never exercised
problems.a: The generated RTL adds timing and interface behavior that the C model never exercised
problems.e: The C test proves the algorithm. Only running the same test against the RTL checks the handshakes, pipelining and scheduling that HLS added.

lesson:
# Data-flow graphs

A data-flow graph (DFG) is the representation every HLS scheduler works on: one node per operation, one edge per value passed from a producer to a consumer. It is built from straight-line code, a basic block, and it says exactly which operations must wait for which. Everything later in the flow, schedule length, mobility, register count, reads off this graph, so a tool designer must be able to build it and measure it by eye.

## Nodes, edges and three-address code

Lower the code to three-address form, where each statement performs one operation on at most two operands: $n_1 = a + b$, $n_2 = n_1 \times c$, $n_3 = n_1 + n_2$. Each statement is a node, labelled with its operation type. Each operand that names an earlier result is an edge from that producer to this consumer; operands that are primary inputs, here $a$, $b$, $c$, are sources outside the graph and add no operation-to-operation edge. In the example, $n_2$ reads $n_1$ (one edge) and $n_3$ reads $n_1$ and $n_2$ (two edges), so the DFG has three operations and three data edges. Because SSA gives every value one definition, the edges can be read directly from the operand names. A DFG of a basic block is acyclic: a value cannot depend on itself inside one execution of the block.

## Depth: the longest dependence chain

The depth of a DFG is the largest number of operations on any path from a source to a sink. With every operation taking one control step, depth is the minimum schedule length even with unlimited hardware, because each operation on the chain must wait for the previous one. Compute it by processing nodes in topological order: the level of a node is one plus the largest level of its predecessors, and sources have level 1. For $n_1 = a + b$, $n_2 = c + d$, $n_3 = n_1 \times n_2$, $n_4 = n_3 + a$, $n_5 = n_2 + b$, the levels are 1, 1, 2, 3, 2, so the depth is 3. This is the same longest-path computation static timing analysis uses, with operation counts in place of delays.

## Sinks, sources and what the graph leaves out

Sources are operations that read only primary inputs; sinks are operations whose result no later operation reads. A sink's value must leave the block, as an output port, a store to memory or a value live into the next block, so sinks mark where results are consumed by the outside. Count them by checking which operation names never appear as an operand. The DFG deliberately omits several things: control flow (it cannot say that only one of two branches runs), the clock (it has no cycles yet), and memory ordering beyond explicit edges (two accesses to the same array need an extra dependence edge if one is a store). Width and operation type ride along as node attributes, which later decide which unit can execute the node and how long it takes.

## Going deeper

De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 3 on graph models; Gajski, Dutt, Wu and Lin, "High-Level Synthesis: Introduction to Chip and System Design" (1992).

problems.e: The operations whose names never appear as an operand are n3, n5, n6, n8, so there are 4 sinks.

label: Control-data-flow graphs
lesson:
# Control-data-flow graphs

Real programs have branches and loops, which a data-flow graph cannot express. The control-data-flow graph (CDFG) is the two-level representation HLS tools use instead: a control-flow graph of basic blocks, each holding an acyclic DFG. It decides where a scheduler can move operations, where the controller needs states and transitions, and which operations can share hardware because they never run together.

## Basic blocks inside a control-flow graph

A basic block is a maximal straight-line run of operations entered only at the top and left only at the bottom. The CDFG has one node per basic block, with control edges for every possible transfer: fall-through, the two arms of a branch, a loop's back edge and its exit. Inside each block sits that block's DFG, which is acyclic. A loop such as 'for i in 0..N-1: s += a[i]' becomes an entry block, a header that tests $i < N$, a body that loads $a[i]$ and adds, and an exit; the cycle lives in the control level as the back edge from body to header. A function with blocks entry, header, body and exit therefore carries four DFGs. The controller FSM that HLS later emits mirrors this structure: states for the steps of each block, transitions along the control edges.

## Branches, if-conversion and exclusive arms

A branch can stay as control, with the controller choosing which arm's states to enter, or be converted into data. If-conversion computes both arms and selects the result with a multiplexer driven by the condition, turning a control dependence into a data dependence and merging the arms into one larger basic block that the scheduler packs freely. The cost is work: both arms execute every time, so two multiplications in different arms both consume multiplier slots even though one result is discarded. When the branch stays as control, the arms are mutually exclusive, and a CDFG-aware binder exploits that: an operation in the then-arm and one in the else-arm can share a single unit even in the same control step, since they never run in the same execution. Loops need a known trip count, or a bound, before the tool can report a fixed latency.

## What the representation lets the scheduler do

A scheduler that works one basic block at a time treats block boundaries as barriers, and loses the chance to fill idle steps with operations from neighbouring blocks. Global techniques move operations across those boundaries: code hoisting, trace and path-based scheduling, and speculation, which executes an operation before the branch that guards it. Speculation is safe only for operations without side effects whose result can be dropped if the branch goes the other way; a store to memory must stay guarded. Loop-carried values, such as an accumulator $s$ updated every iteration, enter the header through a phi node fed from the end of the body. They are not edges inside the body's DFG, which stays acyclic, but they are exactly the recurrences that bound a pipelined loop's initiation interval later. A while-loop with a data-dependent exit forces the controller to test every iteration, so its latency is only known as a range.

## Going deeper

Gajski, Dutt, Wu and Lin, "High-Level Synthesis" (1992), chapter on design representation; Coussy and Morawiec (eds.), "High-Level Synthesis: From Algorithm to Digital Circuit" (2008), chapters on front-end compilation.

A) Four, one per basic block

B) One, merged over the whole function

C) Two, one per branch direction

D) One per operation
problems.a: Four, one per basic block
problems.e: Every basic block carries its own DFG, so there is one per block.

B) Four, one per basic block

C) One, merged over the whole function

problems.a: Four, one per basic block
problems.e: Every basic block carries its own DFG, so there is one per block.

A) Two, one per branch direction

B) One, merged over the whole function

C) Four, one per basic block

D) One per operation
problems.a: Four, one per basic block
problems.e: Every basic block carries its own DFG, so there is one per block.

Two branch arms are mutually exclusive. What sharing opportunity can a CDFG-aware binder exploit?

A) The arms can share a register only if they write the same variable

B) Operations in different arms can share one functional unit even in the same control step

C) Mutually exclusive operations can be deleted

D) Operations in different arms must always use separate units
problems.a: Operations in different arms can share one functional unit even in the same control step

Two branch arms are mutually exclusive. What sharing opportunity can a CDFG-aware binder exploit?

A) Operations in different arms must always use separate units

B) The arms can share a register only if they write the same variable

C) Mutually exclusive operations can be deleted

D) Operations in different arms can share one functional unit even in the same control step
problems.a: Operations in different arms can share one functional unit even in the same control step
problems.e: Only one arm runs in a given execution, so two operations from different arms never actually compete for a unit.

problems.q:
After if-conversion, both branch arms contain a multiplication. What does that cost compared with keeping the branch?

A) It doubles the loop trip count

B) Both multiplications execute every time, using multiplier slots for a result that is discarded

C) The select removes one of the multipliers automatically

D) Nothing, because the discarded multiplication is free
problems.a: Both multiplications execute every time, using multiplier slots for a result that is discarded
problems.e: If-conversion trades control for computation. It pays off when the arms are cheap or units are idle anyway.

problems.q:
A while-loop exits on a data-dependent condition. What does that do to the controller and the latency?

A) While-loops cannot be synthesized at all

B) The controller tests the condition every iteration, so the latency is not fixed at compile time

C) The loop always runs exactly once in hardware

D) Every operation is forced into a single cycle
problems.a: The controller tests the condition every iteration, so the latency is not fixed at compile time
problems.e: The loop becomes a cycle of FSM states with a conditional exit, and the tool can only report a range or a bound for its latency.

problems.q:
A scheduler works one basic block at a time. What opportunity does it lose?

A) Nothing, because blocks never compete for units

B) The ability to chain operations inside a block

C) The ability to bind registers

D) Moving operations across block boundaries to fill idle steps, as global code motion or speculation would
problems.a: Moving operations across block boundaries to fill idle steps, as global code motion or speculation would
problems.e: Block boundaries act as barriers. Global scheduling and speculation move operations across them to shorten the schedule.

problems.q:
A scheduler works one basic block at a time. What opportunity does it lose?

A) The ability to bind registers

B) Nothing, because blocks never compete for units

C) Moving operations across block boundaries to fill idle steps, as global code motion or speculation would

D) The ability to chain operations inside a block
problems.a: Moving operations across block boundaries to fill idle steps, as global code motion or speculation would
problems.e: Block boundaries act as barriers. Global scheduling and speculation move operations across them to shorten the schedule.

label: Lowering C to a CDFG: SSA, memories and widths
lesson:
# Lowering C to a CDFG: SSA, memories and widths

Before any scheduling, the HLS front end turns C into a clean intermediate form: static single assignment, explicit memories for arrays, known bit widths and simplified arithmetic. These lowering decisions fix the size of every unit and the dependences the scheduler must respect, so a tool designer must know what each one buys and what it can break.

## SSA form and phi nodes

In static single assignment form every variable is assigned exactly once in the program text: reassignments get fresh names $x_1, x_2, \dots$ At a join of control flow, where different paths define different versions, SSA inserts a phi node, $x_3 = \phi(x_1, x_2)$, which picks the version from the edge actually taken. SSA makes data-flow graphs trivial to build, because each use names one definition, so def-use edges are explicit. It also maps cleanly onto hardware. A phi at a join that has been if-converted becomes a multiplexer selected by the branch condition, and a phi at a loop header becomes the register that carries a value from one iteration into the next, with a multiplexer choosing between the initial value and the value fed back.

## Arrays, pointers, calls and widths

Each C construct gets a hardware meaning. A large local array becomes an on-chip RAM with one or two ports, not a bank of registers, so the number of accesses per cycle is limited; small arrays may be split into registers by partitioning. Pointers that may alias force the tool to keep their loads and stores in program order, since a store through one may change what a load through the other reads; restrict qualifiers or separate arrays remove that ordering. Function calls are usually inlined so the callee's operations join the caller's DFG and can overlap with it, although a large callee may be kept as a shared sub-module. Bit width is a first-class cost: arbitrary-precision types such as a 12-bit integer make 12-bit adders and registers instead of 32-bit ones, and the area and delay of a multiplier grow quickly with its operand widths.

## Optimizations that reshape the graph

Several compiler passes change the graph the scheduler sees. Constant propagation and strength reduction turn $y \times 8$ into a shift by 3 bits, which is only wiring. Common-subexpression elimination removes repeated computations. Tree-height reduction rebalances associative chains: $((a + b) + c) + d$ has depth 3, while $(a + b) + (c + d)$ has depth 2 with the same three additions, shortening the critical path. On integers this is exact, because two's-complement addition is associative even with wraparound. On floating point it is not, since every addition rounds, so tools reassociate floating-point only when the user permits it. Bitwidth analysis proves ranges: a counter that never exceeds 99 needs $\lceil \log_2 100 \rceil = 7$ bits. Each pass is small, but together they decide the operation count and depth that bound every schedule.

## Going deeper

Cytron et al., "Efficiently computing static single assignment form and the control dependence graph" (ACM TOPLAS, 1991); Kastner, Matai and Neuendorffer, "Parallel Programming for FPGAs" (2018), chapters on arrays and bit widths.

In the RTL produced by HLS, what does a phi node at an if-converted join usually become?

A) A multiplexer selected by the branch condition

B) A FIFO that queues both incoming values

C) An adder that sums both incoming values

D) A flip-flop clocked by the branch condition
problems.a: A multiplexer selected by the branch condition
problems.e: Choosing one of two incoming values by a condition is exactly what a multiplexer does.

problems.q:
In the RTL produced by HLS, what does a phi node at an if-converted join usually become?

A) A flip-flop clocked by the branch condition

B) An adder that sums both incoming values

C) A multiplexer selected by the branch condition

D) A FIFO that queues both incoming values
problems.a: A multiplexer selected by the branch condition
problems.e: Choosing one of two incoming values by a condition is exactly what a multiplexer does.

problems.q:

A) Exactly once in the program text

B) Any number of times, but read only once

C) Once per loop iteration

D) At most twice, once per branch
problems.a: Exactly once in the program text
problems.e: SSA renames every assignment to a fresh name, so each name has exactly one static definition.

problems.q:
Why are function calls often inlined before scheduling?

A) Hardware cannot implement a sub-function as a module

B) Inlining always reduces the number of operations

C) SSA construction requires it

D) Inlining exposes the callee's operations to the caller's schedule so they can overlap and share units
problems.a: Inlining exposes the callee's operations to the caller's schedule so they can overlap and share units
problems.e: A call boundary hides operations from the scheduler. After inlining they join the caller's DFG and can be packed with it.

problems.q:
Two pointer arguments might alias. What does that force an HLS tool to do?

A) Merge both arrays into one register file

B) Delete the stores

C) Fully unroll every loop

D) Keep their loads and stores in program order, because it cannot prove they touch different memory
problems.a: Keep their loads and stores in program order, because it cannot prove they touch different memory
problems.e: Without proof of independence, a store through one pointer may change what a load through the other reads, so the memory dependence must be honored.

problems.q:
A local array 'int buf[1024]' in an FPGA HLS kernel becomes what by default?

A) An on-chip RAM with a limited number of ports

B) An off-chip DRAM buffer

C) 1024 independent registers

D) A FIFO of depth 1024
problems.a: An on-chip RAM with a limited number of ports
problems.e: Large arrays map to block RAM, which serves one or two accesses per cycle. That port limit later bounds the II.

problems.q:
The statement x = y × 8 on integers is simplified before scheduling. What is the cheapest hardware?

A) A left shift by 3 bits, which is only wiring

B) A 256-entry lookup table

C) A chain of eight adders

D) A multiplier with one constant input
problems.a: A left shift by 3 bits, which is only wiring
problems.e: Multiplying by a power of two is a shift, and a constant shift costs no logic at all.

problems.q:
The statement x = y × 8 on integers is simplified before scheduling. What is the cheapest hardware?

A) A chain of eight adders

B) A multiplier with one constant input

C) A left shift by 3 bits, which is only wiring

D) A 256-entry lookup table
problems.a: A left shift by 3 bits, which is only wiring
problems.e: Multiplying by a power of two is a shift, and a constant shift costs no logic at all.

problems.q:
Why does an HLS tool not reassociate floating-point (a + b) + c by default?

A) Reassociation always increases latency

B) C does not allow parentheses in floating-point expressions

C) Floating-point adders cannot be chained

D) Floating-point addition is not associative, so reassociation can change the result
problems.a: Floating-point addition is not associative, so reassociation can change the result
problems.e: Rounding happens at each step, so the order of additions matters. Tools reassociate only when the user permits it.

label: Operation latency and the clock period
lesson:
# Operation latency and the clock period

A scheduler counts in control steps, but operations have delays in nanoseconds. Converting one into the other, given the target clock period and the characterized delay of each operator, is the first quantitative decision of HLS. It decides whether a multiplication is a one-cycle or a three-cycle operation, which in turn sets the critical path, the unit occupancy and the register count of everything downstream.

## From nanoseconds to cycles

Each operator type has a characterized combinational delay for its width on the target technology: a 32-bit adder might take 1.2 ns, a 32-bit multiplier 6 ns. If the result must be registered before use and register overhead is ignored, an operation with delay $d$ at clock period $T$ needs $\lceil d / T \rceil$ cycles. A 7.3 ns multiplier at a 3 ns clock needs $\lceil 2.43 \rceil = 3$ cycles. The ceiling is the cost of quantization: the third cycle is mostly idle, but it still costs a whole cycle. In practice the usable part of the period is $T$ minus the register's clock-to-q and setup time, plus a margin for clock uncertainty, so the tool divides by that usable time instead. The operator library that supplies these delays is one of the most important inputs an HLS engine has.

## Latency of a registered chain

When every result is registered and nothing is chained, a chain of dependent operations takes the sum of each operation's cycle count. Delays of 4, 2.8 and 4.9 ns at a 4 ns clock cost 1, 1 and 2 cycles, so the chain takes 4 cycles, or 16 ns, although its total combinational delay is only 11.7 ns. The wasted 4.3 ns is the quantization loss of three separate roundings. This is why schedulers chain short operations into one cycle when they fit, and why HLS reports often show a latency in cycles that looks larger than the raw arithmetic would suggest. A multicycle operation also occupies its unit for several cycles, unless the unit is pipelined, which changes how many operations a unit can serve per cycle.

## Choosing the clock period

A faster clock is not automatically better. The total time of a chain is its cycle count times the period, and the rounding interacts with the period. With delays 9, 7.5 and 5.6 ns, a 2.5 ns clock gives $4 + 3 + 3 = 10$ cycles, 25 ns, while a 5 ns clock gives $2 + 2 + 2 = 6$ cycles, 30 ns. Another chain might favour the slower clock. Beyond rounding, a faster clock adds pipeline registers, area and power, and raises the register overhead's share of each cycle. Designers usually fix the period from the surrounding system and let HLS fit the operations to it; a design-space explorer may sweep the period as one more knob. Either way, the latency and throughput numbers an HLS report shows depend on the period at which the tool was asked to schedule.

## Going deeper

De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 5; the operator characterization sections of the AMD Vitis HLS user guide (UG1399).

prereqs: Operation latency and the clock period
lesson:
# ASAP and ALAP scheduling

ASAP and ALAP are the two extreme schedules of a data-flow graph with unlimited resources: every operation as early as its inputs allow, or as late as the latency bound allows. They take linear time, they give the minimum schedule length, and the window between them, each operation's time frame, is the input to list scheduling, force-directed scheduling and every ILP or SDC formulation.

## As soon as possible

Number control steps from 1. An operation that starts in step $s$ with latency $l$ occupies steps $s$ to $s + l - 1$, and a consumer may start in step $s + l$. ASAP visits the operations in topological order: a source starts in step 1, and any other operation starts at $\max_p (s_p + l_p)$ over its predecessors $p$. With additions of 1 step and multiplications of 2, take $n_1 = a + d$, $n_2 = d \times d$, $n_3 = n_1 + n_2$. Then $n_1$ and $n_2$ start in step 1, and $n_3$ waits for the later of $1 + 1 = 2$ and $1 + 2 = 3$, so it starts in step 3. This is a longest-path computation on the DAG with edge weights equal to the producer latencies, done in one pass over the graph.

## The minimum schedule length

The ASAP schedule finishes when its last operation finishes, in step $\max_i (s_i + l_i - 1)$. No schedule can be shorter, because each operation already starts at the earliest moment its dependences allow; this number is the latency-weighted critical path of the DFG. Continuing the example with $n_4 = n_3 + g$, $n_4$ starts in step 4 and ends in step 4, so the block needs at least 4 steps. Unlimited hardware is assumed: ASAP may put five multiplications in the same step. The schedule length is therefore a lower bound that real, resource-limited schedules can only match or exceed, and it is the natural latency target to start from. A designer who needs fewer steps must change the graph, by tree-height reduction or chaining, not the scheduler.

## As late as possible

Given a latency bound of $L$ steps, ALAP schedules backwards. A sink starts at $L - l + 1$, so that it finishes exactly in step $L$; any other operation starts at $\min_c (s_c) - l_i$ over its consumers $c$. Visit the operations in reverse topological order. With $L$ equal to the critical path, operations on the critical path get the same start in ASAP and ALAP; with a looser bound, every operation can slide later. The pair gives each operation a time frame $[\mathrm{ASAP}_i, \mathrm{ALAP}_i]$ of legal start steps, assuming unlimited resources. ALAP also has a practical use: placing operations late shortens the lifetimes of values that feed them from far away, and it is the classic seed for list-scheduling priorities.

## Going deeper

De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 5, sections on unconstrained and latency-constrained scheduling.

# Mobility and the critical path

Mobility, also called slack, is how far an operation can move in time without stretching the schedule: its ALAP start minus its ASAP start. It is the single most used number in HLS scheduling: zero-mobility operations form the critical path, list schedulers use it for priority, force-directed scheduling turns it into probabilities, and ILP models use it to decide how many variables to create.

## ALAP minus ASAP

Compute the ASAP schedule, choose a latency bound $L$, compute ALAP under $L$, and subtract: $\mu_i = \mathrm{ALAP}_i - \mathrm{ASAP}_i$. The time frame $[\mathrm{ASAP}_i, \mathrm{ALAP}_i]$ has $\mu_i + 1$ legal start steps. With additions of 1 step and multiplications of 2, consider $n_1 = a + b$, $n_2 = c \times d$, $n_3 = n_1 + n_2$, with $L$ equal to the critical path of 3 steps. ASAP gives 1, 1, 3. ALAP gives $n_3 = 3$, $n_2 = 3 - 2 = 1$ and $n_1 = 3 - 1 = 2$. So $n_1$ has mobility 1, while $n_2$ and $n_3$ have mobility 0. A negative mobility for any operation would mean the bound $L$ is shorter than the critical path, which is infeasible. Mobility is computed in linear time from the two passes, so tools recompute it after every scheduling decision as frames shrink.

## Zero mobility marks the critical path

When $L$ equals the critical-path length, the operations with zero mobility are exactly those on some longest path. They cannot move at all: delaying any of them by one step delays the end of the schedule. Every other operation has room. Counting zero-mobility operations tells you how constrained a block is. A long chain where every operation is critical leaves the scheduler no freedom, so resource sharing must come from elsewhere; a wide, shallow graph with many mobile operations can be squeezed onto few units. List schedulers exploit this by scheduling low-mobility operations first, since postponing them is what lengthens schedules. The critical path also tells a designer where to apply tree-height reduction or chaining to shorten the latency.

## Relaxing the latency bound

If the bound grows from the critical path $L_0$ to $L_0 + r$, ASAP does not change, because it ignores the bound, and every ALAP start shifts later by exactly $r$, because the backward recursion starts $r$ steps later at every sink and subtracts the same latencies. So every mobility grows by exactly $r$: an operation with mobility 0 at $L_0$ has mobility $r$, and one with mobility 2 has $2 + r$. Relaxing the bound is how a designer trades latency for area: wider frames let the scheduler spread operations of one type across more steps and use fewer units. It also grows every formulation built on frames. A time-indexed ILP has one variable per operation per frame step, so its size grows by $r$ variables per operation.

## Going deeper

De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 5; Gajski, Dutt, Wu and Lin, "High-Level Synthesis" (1992), chapter on scheduling.

label: Resource lower bounds on schedule length
prereqs: Operation latency and the clock period
lesson:
# Resource lower bounds on schedule length

Before running a scheduler, a tool can bound how short any schedule could be from two simple counts: the critical path and the work each unit type must do. These bounds are instant to compute, they tell the designer whether a latency target is even possible with a given allocation, and branch-and-bound schedulers use them to prune.

## Counting work per unit type

Suppose a block has $n_k$ operations of type $k$, each occupying a unit for one step, and the allocation provides $a_k$ units of that type. Each step serves at most $a_k$ of them, so the operations of type $k$ alone need at least $\lceil n_k / a_k \rceil$ steps, whatever the dependences. Twenty-three multiplications on four multipliers need at least $\lceil 23 / 4 \rceil = 6$ steps. This bound ignores the graph completely, and that is its strength: it holds for every schedule, so a latency target below it is infeasible with this allocation, and the tool can say so before scheduling. Reading it the other way, a target of $L$ steps needs at least $\lceil n_k / L \rceil$ units of type $k$, which is the starting point of allocation.

## Multicycle operations occupy units longer

If an operation of type $k$ takes $l_k$ steps on a non-pipelined unit, the unit is busy for all of them, so the type needs $n_k l_k$ unit-steps of work. With $a_k$ units supplying $a_k$ unit-steps per step, the bound becomes $\lceil n_k l_k / a_k \rceil$. Ten two-step multiplications on three multipliers need at least $\lceil 20 / 3 \rceil = 7$ steps. A fully pipelined unit accepts a new operation every step, so its occupancy is one step and the original bound returns, although the last results still arrive $l_k - 1$ steps later. This is the first place where the difference between latency and occupancy matters; it reappears in modulo scheduling, where occupancy rather than latency determines how many operations fit in one initiation interval.

## Combining the bounds

A schedule must respect every bound at once, so the best simple lower bound is the maximum of the critical-path length and the per-type bounds: $L \ge \max(L_{cp}, \lceil n_{add} / a_{add} \rceil, \lceil n_{mul} / a_{mul} \rceil)$. For a block with a critical path of 4 steps, 7 additions on 2 adders and 5 multiplications on 1 multiplier, the bound is $\max(4, 4, 5) = 5$. A real scheduler may need more, because dependences and resources interact: operations may be ready only in steps where the units are already busy. Exact schedulers such as branch and bound use sharper versions of these bounds on partial schedules to prune; list schedulers simply compare their result against this bound to judge how far from optimal they might be.

## Going deeper

De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 5, section on resource-constrained scheduling; Hu, "Parallel sequencing and assembly line problems" (Operations Research, 1961).

lesson:
# List scheduling

List scheduling is the workhorse heuristic for resource-constrained scheduling: walk the control steps in order and, in each, fill the free units with the most urgent ready operations. Resource-constrained scheduling is NP-hard in general, but list scheduling runs in near-linear time, is easy to extend, and is close to optimal on most real blocks, which is why nearly every HLS tool contains a version of it.

## Priority by distance to the sink

A list scheduler needs a priority that says which ready operation matters most. The classic choice is the height of an operation: the length of the longest path from it to any sink, counted in steps and including the operation itself. With unit latencies, compute it in reverse topological order: a sink has height 1, and every other operation has one plus the largest height among its consumers. An operation with a large height starts a long chain, so delaying it is likely to delay the whole schedule. Height is closely related to mobility: under a latency bound equal to the critical path $L$, the ALAP start of an operation is $L - h + 1$ when latencies are one, so sorting by largest height is the same as sorting by earliest ALAP. Other priorities, such as smallest mobility or most successors, are common variants.

## Stepping through the schedule

Start at step 1 with nothing scheduled. In each step, the ready list holds the unscheduled operations whose predecessors have all finished. Sort it by priority, ties to the lower-numbered operation, and for each unit type assign ready operations of that type to free units until the units or the candidates run out. Then advance one step. Take $n_1 = a + b$, $n_2 = c + d$, $n_3 = n_1 + n_2$, $n_4 = n_1 \times n_2$, $n_5 = n_4 + e$ with one adder and one multiplier, unit latencies. Heights are 3, 3, 1, 2, 1. Step 1 schedules $n_1$; step 2 schedules $n_2$; step 3 has $n_3$ and $n_4$ ready, and they use different units, so both go; step 4 runs $n_5$. The schedule takes 4 steps, against a critical path of 3, because the single adder serialized $n_1$ and $n_2$.

## Multicycle units and the quality of the result

With multicycle operations, the scheduler tracks which units are still busy. A non-pipelined multiplier with a latency of 2 started in step 3 is unavailable in step 4, and its consumers become ready in step 5. The algorithm is otherwise unchanged. List scheduling is greedy: it never delays a ready operation to leave room for a more important one that becomes ready a step later, so it can miss the optimum. Hu's algorithm, list scheduling by height, is optimal for unit-latency trees on identical units, but general graphs with several unit types have no such guarantee. In practice tools compare the result against the lower bound from the critical path and the resource counts; if they match, the schedule is provably optimal, and if not, the gap tells how much an exact method could win.

## Going deeper

De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 5, section on list scheduling; Hu, "Parallel sequencing and assembly line problems" (Operations Research, 1961).

prereqs: Resource lower bounds on schedule length
lesson:
# Latency-constrained scheduling and unit counts

The dual of resource-constrained scheduling fixes the latency and asks for the fewest units. This is the usual situation when a throughput or deadline requirement is given and area is to be minimized. Every schedule implies a unit count, the busiest step's demand, and different legal schedules within the same latency imply very different areas.

## The unit count a schedule implies

Given a fixed schedule with single-cycle operations, the datapath needs as many units of type $k$ as the largest number of type-$k$ operations sharing one step: $a_k = \max_s |\{ i : \mathrm{type}(i) = k, s_i = s \}|$. In an ASAP schedule that places three multiplications in step 1 and one in each later step, three multipliers are needed even though most of them idle after step 1. ASAP tends to bunch operations early, because everything ready starts at once, so it usually implies more units than necessary. For multicycle non-pipelined operations, count the operations whose busy interval covers the step instead of only those starting in it. This count is what binding later realizes: it is the minimum number of cliques in the compatibility graph of that type.

## The counting lower bound under a latency target

Whatever the dependences, $n_k$ single-cycle operations of type $k$ in $L$ steps need at least $\lceil n_k / L \rceil$ units, since $a$ units serve at most $aL$ operations. Fifteen multiplications in 9 steps need at least $\lceil 15 / 9 \rceil = 2$ multipliers. The bound is achieved only if the operations can be spread evenly, which dependences may prevent: if all fifteen sit in two dependent layers, at least eight must share a step. Still, the bound is the right first estimate of area for a latency target, and it is what a designer uses to size the allocation before running a scheduler. A larger $L$ lowers it, which is the basic latency-area trade-off of HLS.

## Where operations sit inside their frames

Moving operations within their time frames changes the implied unit count without changing the latency. Placing every operation at its ALAP step bunches work at the end, just as ASAP bunches it at the start; for a block whose multiplications have frames spread over several steps, both extremes can need two multipliers where a balanced placement needs one. Latency-constrained schedulers therefore look for a placement that flattens each type's per-step demand. Force-directed scheduling does it with distribution graphs, ILP formulations minimize the unit count directly subject to the latency bound, and simple iterative methods repeatedly move an operation from the busiest step to a less busy step inside its frame. The question in every case is the same: which step within its frame should each operation take so that the peak demand is lowest.

## Going deeper

prereqs: Expected value of a random variable
lesson:
# Force-directed scheduling

Force-directed scheduling, introduced by Paulin and Knight, attacks latency-constrained scheduling by balancing the expected demand on each unit type across control steps. It treats each unscheduled operation as spread uniformly over its time frame, sums those probabilities into distribution graphs, and repeatedly fixes the operation whose placement best flattens them. It is the classic example of a scheduler that reasons about all operations at once rather than greedily.

## Time frames as probabilities

Fix a latency bound $L$ and compute each operation's frame $[\mathrm{ASAP}_i, \mathrm{ALAP}_i]$, which has width $w_i = \mu_i + 1$. Before any decision, assume operation $i$ is equally likely to start in any step of its frame: $p_i(s) = 1 / w_i$ for $s$ inside the frame and 0 outside. An operation with frame $[4, 6]$ has probability $1/3 \approx 0.33$ in each of steps 4, 5 and 6, and 0 in step 3. A critical operation has width 1, so its probability is 1 in its only step: it is already decided. The model ignores dependences between the probabilities of connected operations, which is a simplification the algorithm corrects by recomputing frames after every decision.

## Distribution graphs

For each unit type $k$ and step $s$, the distribution graph sums the probabilities of the type-$k$ operations: $DG_k(s) = \sum_{i \in k} p_i(s)$. It estimates how many type-$k$ units step $s$ will need. With multiplications m1 in $[1, 3]$, m2 in $[4, 4]$ and m3 in $[1, 4]$ under $L = 4$, step 2 receives $1/3$ from m1 and $1/4$ from m3, so $DG(2) = 0.58$; step 4 receives 1 from m2 and $1/4$ from m3, so $DG(4) = 1.25$. A peak in the distribution graph signals a step where multiplications will collide and force an extra multiplier. The goal of the algorithm is a schedule whose distribution graphs are as flat as possible, since the peak of the final, fully decided graph is the number of units needed.

## Self-force and the iteration

Fixing operation $i$ in step $j$ changes its probability from $1/w_i$ everywhere in its frame to 1 at $j$ and 0 elsewhere. The self-force of that choice is $F_i(j) = \sum_s DG_k(s)\,\Delta p_i(s) = DG_k(j) - \frac{1}{w_i} \sum_{s \in \text{frame}} DG_k(s)$: the distribution value at $j$ minus the average over the frame. A negative force means $j$ is a quieter step than average, so placing the operation there flattens the graph. The full algorithm adds predecessor and successor forces, because fixing $i$ shrinks the frames of its neighbours, then fixes the operation and step with the lowest total force, recomputes frames and distribution graphs, and repeats until everything is placed. Each iteration costs a full recomputation, which makes the method roughly cubic in the number of operations.

# ILP and SDC scheduling

Exact scheduling is written as an integer linear program: binary variables say which step each operation starts in, and linear constraints encode uniqueness, dependences and resources. ILP gives optimal schedules for small blocks but scales poorly. The system-of-difference-constraints (SDC) formulation, from Cong and Zhang, keeps only constraints of the form $s_j - s_i \ge c$, whose LP relaxation is integral, and became the scheduling core of several commercial and open HLS tools.

## The time-indexed formulation

Introduce $x_{i,s} \in \{0, 1\}$, equal to 1 when operation $i$ starts in step $s$. Only steps inside the frame $[\mathrm{ASAP}_i, \mathrm{ALAP}_i]$ are allowed, so operation $i$ contributes $\mu_i + 1$ variables. Six operations with frames of widths 2, 1, 3, 1, 2 and 2 under a 5-step bound need $2 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 11$ variables, instead of $6 \times 5 = 30$ for the naive model over all steps. This is why mobility matters for exact methods: the tighter the frames, the smaller the integer program. The start time of operation $i$ is the linear expression $s_i = \sum_s s\, x_{i,s}$, which lets dependences be written on start times while the decision itself stays binary. Tight frames also strengthen the LP relaxation that branch and bound solves at each node, so good bounds and small models go together.

## Constraints and objective

Three families of constraints define a legal schedule. Unique start: $\sum_s x_{i,s} = 1$ for every operation, one constraint each. Precedence: $s_j \ge s_i + l_i$ for every edge $i \to j$, one constraint per edge, written on the start-time expressions. Resources: for every step $s$ and unit type $k$, the operations of type $k$ busy in step $s$ number at most $a_k$, which for single-cycle operations is $\sum_{i \in k} x_{i,s} \le a_k$; that is one constraint per step per type. A block of 7 operations, 11 edges, a 4-step bound and 3 types has $7 + 11 + 12 = 30$ constraints. The objective is either the latency, with the $a_k$ fixed, or the weighted unit count $\sum_k c_k a_k$ with the $a_k$ as integer variables, with the latency fixed. Branch and bound solves it exactly, at exponential worst-case cost.

## The SDC formulation

SDC drops the binary variables and keeps one integer start time $s_i$ per operation. Every constraint is a difference: dependences become $s_j - s_i \ge l_i$, a latency bound becomes $s_{sink} - s_{source} \le L$, and timing constraints for chaining become $s_j - s_i \ge 1$ whenever the combinational delay from the start of $i$ through $j$ exceeds the clock period. On a chain with delays 3, 3, 3 and 1 ns and a 6 ns clock, the pairs (o1, o3), (o1, o4) and (o2, o4) exceed 6 ns and get such constraints. The constraint matrix of a difference system is totally unimodular, so the LP relaxation has integral optimal vertices and an LP solver returns an integer schedule in polynomial time. Resource constraints are not differences; SDC handles them heuristically, by adding ordering constraints between operations that compete for a unit.

# Solving SDC schedules by longest paths

A system of difference constraints is a graph problem in disguise. Each constraint $s_j - s_i \ge w$ is a weighted edge, the least feasible schedule is the longest-path distance from a source, and infeasibility is a positive cycle. Seeing SDC this way lets a tool designer solve small systems by hand, explain why a latency constraint fails, and understand why SDC scheduling is fast.

## Constraints as a weighted graph

Make one vertex per start variable. A constraint $s_j - s_i \ge w$ becomes an edge $i \to j$ with weight $w$. With all starts at least 0, the smallest feasible value of each $s_j$ is the longest-path distance to $j$, starting every vertex at 0: $s_j = \max(0, \max_{i \to j} (s_i + w_{ij}))$. For forward constraints only, the graph is a DAG and one pass in topological order solves it. Take $s_2 - s_1 \ge 2$, $s_3 - s_1 \ge 1$, $s_4 - s_2 \ge 1$ and $s_4 - s_3 \ge 3$. Then $s_1 = 0$, $s_2 = 2$, $s_3 = 1$ and $s_4 = \max(2 + 1, 1 + 3) = 4$. These are exactly the ASAP starts when the weights are latencies, so ASAP is the simplest SDC solution. The same relaxation, run backwards from a latency bound, gives the ALAP starts as the latest feasible values.

## Upper bounds become backward edges

A maximum-latency constraint $s_j - s_i \le c$ is rewritten as $s_i - s_j \ge -c$: an edge from $j$ back to $i$ with weight $-c$. It says $s_i \ge s_j - c$, so if other constraints push $s_j$ late, $s_i$ is dragged later too, to stay within $c$ steps of it. In the example, adding $s_4 - s_2 \le 1$ gives $s_2 \ge s_4 - 1 = 3$, so $s_2$ rises from 2 to 3 and the system is re-relaxed. The graph now has cycles, so a single topological pass no longer suffices; Bellman-Ford relaxation, repeated until nothing changes, finds the least solution in $O(VE)$ time. Such constraints model throughput requirements, I/O timing relative to a start signal, and the maximum separation between two operations that share a register.

## Feasibility and positive cycles

A difference system is feasible exactly when its constraint graph has no cycle of positive total weight. Around a cycle the constraints add up to $0 \ge \sum w$, which fails if the sum is positive; Bellman-Ford detects this as relaxation that never stops. For a latency constraint $s_j - s_i \le c$, the cycle is the longest forward path from $i$ to $j$, of weight $P$, closed by the backward edge of weight $-c$, so the system is feasible if and only if $c \ge P$. With $P = 4$ from $s_1$ to $s_4$, the smallest allowed $c$ is 4: the designer's latency target is infeasible below the critical path between those two operations. This is how an SDC scheduler explains an infeasible constraint: it reports the positive cycle, which names the chain of operations that cannot be squeezed.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Operation chaining

Chaining places several dependent operations in one clock cycle when their combined delay fits, instead of registering every result. It cuts latency and registers, and it is why an HLS schedule is not simply the DFG depth in cycles. The scheduler must know operator delays, register overhead and the clock period, and it must stop chaining before the cycle overflows.

## Usable time in one cycle

A register-to-register path must fit in the clock period minus the register overhead: clock-to-q of the launching register, setup of the capturing one, and any margin for clock uncertainty. With a 10 ns clock and 0.5 ns of overhead, 9.5 ns of logic fits per cycle. Operations chained in one cycle add their delays: an adder of 1.6 ns followed by a multiplier of 5.7 ns uses 7.3 ns, and a further 1.8 ns adder brings it to 9.1 ns, still within 9.5. A fourth operation of 5.4 ns would exceed it and must start a new cycle. Counting how many leading operations of a chain fit in the first cycle is the basic chaining decision. The delays come from the same operator characterization that converts multicycle operations to cycle counts.

## Packing a chain into cycles

For a single chain of operations in fixed order, greedy packing is optimal: fill each cycle with as many next operations as fit, then start a new one. The delays 0.9, 1.0, 2.8, 1.4 and 1.7 ns with 4.7 ns usable per cycle pack as $0.9 + 1.0 + 2.8 = 4.7$ in the first cycle and $1.4 + 1.7 = 3.1$ in the second, two cycles instead of five. Without chaining, each operation takes its own cycle, so the saving is the difference, three cycles here. In a general DFG the scheduler chains along the edges, tracking for each operation the arrival time of its inputs within the current cycle, which is a small static timing analysis performed during scheduling. SDC schedulers encode the same rule as difference constraints between pairs of operations whose combined delay exceeds the period.

## When chaining hurts

Chaining trades clock period headroom for latency. Every chained path is a long combinational path, so the estimate must be accurate: operator delays in HLS libraries are pre-layout numbers, and wires, fanout and multiplexers added by binding lengthen the real path. An optimistic chain that fits by 0.1 ns in the HLS model can fail timing after placement, which is why tools apply a clock uncertainty margin. Chaining also interacts with sharing: an operation chained behind a shared unit inherits that unit's input multiplexer delay. And with no registers between chained operations there is no place to retime later. When delays are uncertain, a tool may chain conservatively, for example only short operations such as additions and logic, and leave multiplications registered.

## Going deeper

De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 5; Cong and Zhang, "An efficient and versatile scheduling algorithm based on SDC formulation" (DAC, 2006), section on operation chaining.

lesson:
# Multicycle and pipelined functional units

Many operators take several cycles: multipliers, dividers, floating-point units, memory reads. Whether such a unit is pipelined, accepting a new operation every cycle, or not, blocking until it finishes, changes how many operations it serves and therefore the whole schedule. The distinction between latency, the cycles to a result, and occupancy, the cycles the unit is busy, is the key to resource bounds and modulo scheduling.

## Non-pipelined units

A non-pipelined unit with latency $L$ accepts an operation, computes for $L$ cycles and only then accepts the next. With $u$ such units and $n$ independent operations all ready in step 1, the units work in rounds of $L$ cycles, each round finishing $u$ operations, so the last result is available at the end of step $\lceil n / u \rceil L$. Thirteen multiplications on three 6-cycle multipliers take 5 rounds, finishing in step 30. Occupancy equals latency here, so the resource bound on schedule length is $\lceil n L / u \rceil$, and every operation ties up its unit for the full duration. Non-pipelined iterative units, such as a sequential divider that produces one quotient bit per cycle, are small but slow; their area advantage is what justifies the blocking.

## Fully pipelined units

A pipelined unit splits its logic into $L$ stages separated by registers and accepts a new operation every cycle, so its occupancy is one cycle while its latency stays $L$. With $u$ units and $n$ independent operations, the last issue happens in step $\lceil n / u \rceil$ and its result appears $L - 1$ steps later, in step $\lceil n / u \rceil + L - 1$. Ten multiplications on two 6-cycle pipelined multipliers issue in steps 1 to 5 and finish in step 10, against step 30 for the non-pipelined case. For independent work the pipeline hides latency almost completely. For a dependent chain it hides nothing: each operation still waits $L$ cycles for its input. That asymmetry is why recurrences, not resources, often limit pipelined loops.

## Partially pipelined units

Between the two extremes sits a unit with an initiation interval $p$: it accepts a new operation every $p$ cycles, so occupancy is $p$ and latency is $L$, with $1 \le p \le L$. A divider with $L = 4$ and $p = 2$ issuing nine divisions on three units issues in steps 1, 3 and 5 and finishes the last in step $5 + 4 - 1 = 8$. In general the completion step is $(\lceil n / u \rceil - 1) p + L$. Floating-point units and memory controllers often look like this, and HLS operator libraries record both numbers per operator. Schedulers must use occupancy for resource conflicts and latency for dependences; confusing the two either overbooks a unit or wastes cycles waiting for results that are already available.

## Going deeper

De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 5; Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach", the appendix on pipelining with multicycle operations.

# Allocation of functional units

Allocation chooses how many units of each type the datapath contains and which unit types to use at all. It sets the area budget that scheduling works within, and it is where the first latency-area trade-off is made. Allocation decisions also include choosing between specialized units and multi-function units, such as separate adders and subtractors or combined add/subtract units.

## Datapath area from an allocation

Each unit type has a cost from the operator library, measured in LUTs and DSP blocks on an FPGA or in cell area on an ASIC. The functional-unit and register area of an allocation is $\sum_k a_k c_k$ over unit counts $a_k$ and costs $c_k$. Four adders of 80 units, two multipliers of 300 and six registers of 60 cost $320 + 600 + 360 = 1280$ units. Multipliers usually dominate, which is why allocation focuses on them, but the count of registers and the multiplexers that sharing introduces can matter as much in heavily shared designs. Interconnect is decided later by binding, so allocation-time area is a lower estimate; a design with fewer units but many shared multiplexers can end up larger than one with more units.

## Minimum allocation for a latency target

Under a latency bound of $L$ steps, $n_k$ single-cycle operations of type $k$ need at least $\lceil n_k / L \rceil$ units, so the smallest functional-unit area any schedule could use is $\sum_k \lceil n_k / L \rceil c_k$. Eleven additions and nine multiplications in 8 steps need at least 2 adders and 2 multipliers; at 60 and 700 units that is 1520. Whether a schedule reaches this allocation depends on the dependences, but it is the natural first allocation to try, increasing a type's count only when the scheduler cannot meet the latency. Sweeping $L$ traces the latency-area curve: halving the latency roughly doubles the units of every type that is resource-bound, while types with few operations stay at one unit.

## Specialized or multi-function units

A combined unit can execute several operation types, at a cost higher than any one specialized unit but lower than two. With five additions and three subtractions in 2 steps, separate units need $\lceil 5/2 \rceil = 3$ adders and $\lceil 3/2 \rceil = 2$ subtractors; at 30 and 50 units that is 190. Combined add/subtract units of 40 units each need $\lceil 8/2 \rceil = 4$, costing 160. Pooling operation types smooths the per-step demand, since a step heavy in additions and light in subtractions no longer wastes a subtractor. The cost is a function-select signal from the controller, slightly more delay through the unit, and sometimes worse scheduling flexibility. Choosing unit types is part of allocation, and HLS tools expose it through resource directives.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Value lifetimes and register count

Once operations are scheduled, every intermediate value that crosses a clock edge needs a register for some interval of steps: its lifetime. The number of registers a datapath needs is the largest number of lifetimes that overlap in any step. Computing lifetimes is the first step of register binding, and it is how a scheduling decision turns into register area.

## From a schedule to lifetimes

A value written at the end of step $d$ is first readable in step $d + 1$, and it must be held through its last read in step $u$. Its register lifetime is the interval of steps $[d + 1, u]$. A value written in step 1 and read in step 5 occupies a register during steps 2 to 5; a value written in step 3 and read in step 4 occupies one only during step 4. Values chained within a cycle never reach a register and have no lifetime at all. Primary inputs and outputs are usually held in interface registers and handled separately. Lifetimes depend on the schedule: moving a consumer earlier or a producer later shortens a lifetime, which is one reason schedulers sometimes prefer ALAP placement for operations that consume long-lived inputs.

## Counting live values

A value is live in step $t$ when $t$ lies in its lifetime. The number of values live in step $t$ is the register demand of that step, and the datapath needs at least the maximum demand over all steps. With lifetimes $[2, 5]$, $[8, 8]$, $[3, 5]$, $[4, 7]$ and $[7, 7]$, step 4 has three live values and so does step 5, while step 7 has two; the maximum is 3. For values that each live in one contiguous interval, this maximum is also achievable: the left-edge algorithm binds the values into exactly that many registers. That is a special property of intervals; values that wrap around a loop's back edge form circular arcs, and then the maximum overlap is only a lower bound.

## Values with several readers

A value read by several operations lives until its last reader, not its first. If $v_1$ is written in step 1 and read in steps 3 and 5, its lifetime is $[2, 5]$, even though one reader finished early. Fan-out therefore stretches lifetimes, and a scheduler that places one late consumer of a heavily used value can raise the register count of the whole block. Tools have two remedies: reschedule the late consumer earlier inside its frame, or recompute the value near the late consumer when the operation is cheap, which trades a unit cycle for a register. Loop-carried values live from their definition in one iteration to their use in the next, so in a pipelined loop their lifetimes are measured modulo the initiation interval, which is where rotating register files come from in software pipelining.

## Going deeper

Kurdahi and Parker, "REAL: a program for register allocation" (DAC, 1987); De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 6.

# Register binding by the left-edge algorithm

The left-edge algorithm assigns values with interval lifetimes to registers using the minimum possible number of registers. It was invented for channel routing, assigning wire segments to tracks, and Kurdahi and Parker carried it into register allocation for HLS. It is simple, runs in $O(n \log n)$, and is optimal for intervals, which makes it the standard register binder in straight-line code.

## Sort by left edge and fill registers

Sort the values by the start of their lifetime, the left edge, breaking ties by a fixed order such as value number. Process them in that order. Give each value the lowest-numbered register whose last value ended before this one starts; if no register is free, open a new one. For lifetimes $v_1: [1, 1]$, $v_6: [1, 2]$, $v_5: [1, 2]$, $v_7: [2, 3]$, $v_2: [3, 5]$, $v_3: [4, 4]$ and $v_4: [5, 5]$, sorted order is $v_1, v_5, v_6, v_7, v_2, v_3, v_4$. Then $v_1 \to R_1$, $v_5 \to R_2$, $v_6 \to R_3$ (both earlier registers are busy in step 1), $v_7 \to R_1$, $v_2 \to R_2$, $v_3 \to R_1$ and $v_4 \to R_1$. Three registers are used, which matches the three values live together in step 1. The only data structure needed is the list of each register's last end time, so the pass is a sort followed by a linear scan.

## Why it is optimal

Suppose the algorithm opens register $R_k$ for a value $v$ starting in step $t$. Every earlier register is busy at $t$, holding a value that started at or before $t$ (sorting guarantees that) and ends at or after $t$. So $k$ values, including $v$, are live in step $t$, and at least $k$ registers are necessary. The number of registers used therefore equals the maximum number of overlapping lifetimes, the lower bound. Equivalently, left edge is a greedy coloring of an interval graph in order of left endpoints, and such a coloring uses exactly the clique number of colors. Filling one register at a time, taking from the sorted list every value that fits after the previous one, yields the same assignment, which is the form in which the channel-routing literature states it.

## Why the sort matters

The sort is the whole trick. First-fit in an arbitrary order can use more registers than the maximum overlap. Take $a: [1, 2]$, $b: [4, 5]$, $c: [3, 6]$ and $d: [2, 3]$, processed in that listed order. First-fit puts $a$ and then $b$ in $R_1$; $c$ overlaps $b$, so it opens $R_2$; $d$ overlaps $a$ in $R_1$ and $c$ in $R_2$, so it opens $R_3$. Yet no step has more than two live values. Sorted by left edge, the order is $a, d, c, b$, giving $a \to R_1$, $d \to R_2$, $c \to R_1$ and $b \to R_2$: two registers. The sort prevents the failure because no value processed later can start before one already placed, so whenever every register is busy at a value's start, each is busy with a value live in that very step. Left edge minimizes registers only; it ignores which values share a register, which decides multiplexer cost, so practical binders weight the choice of register to reduce interconnect.

## Going deeper

Hashimoto and Stevens, "Wire routing by optimizing channel assignment within large apertures" (DAC, 1971); Kurdahi and Parker, "REAL: a program for register allocation" (DAC, 1987).

prereqs: Register binding by the left-edge algorithm
lesson:
# Register binding as interval-graph coloring

Register binding is graph coloring: values are vertices, an edge joins two values that are live at the same time, and registers are colors. For straight-line schedules this interference graph is an interval graph, a perfect graph, so coloring is easy and the minimum number of registers equals the largest clique. Knowing why tells a tool designer when binding stays polynomial and when it becomes NP-hard.

## The interference graph

Draw one vertex per value and an edge between two values whose lifetimes share a step: $[a, b]$ and $[c, d]$ overlap when $a \le d$ and $c \le b$. Two adjacent values can never share a register, and two non-adjacent values can. Count edges by testing every pair: for seven values that is 21 tests. For lifetimes $[4, 5]$, $[3, 3]$, $[2, 4]$, $[4, 6]$, $[3, 3]$, $[5, 6]$ and $[3, 3]$, the three values living only in step 3 all overlap each other and $[2, 4]$, and so on. An interference graph of this kind, built from intervals on a line, is an interval graph. The same structure appears in register allocation for software compilers, where the program's control flow can make it far more general.

## Chromatic number equals the largest clique

A set of intervals that pairwise overlap has a common point, so every clique of an interval graph corresponds to a step where all its values are live, and the largest clique is the maximum overlap. Interval graphs are perfect: for them and every induced subgraph, the chromatic number equals the clique number. So the fewest registers is exactly the maximum number of values live in one step, and a greedy coloring in order of left endpoints, the left-edge algorithm, achieves it in polynomial time. For general graphs, deciding whether three colors suffice is NP-complete, which is why compiler register allocators fall back on heuristics such as Chaitin-style simplification. HLS binding stays easy only as long as lifetimes stay intervals.

## Checking a binding and leaving the interval world

A binding is a coloring, and it is legal when no edge joins two values with the same register. To check a proposed binding, list for each register the values assigned to it and test those pairs for overlap; each overlapping pair is a conflict that would corrupt one value. Conflicts creep in when a binder changes assignments to reduce multiplexers and forgets a lifetime. Lifetimes stop being intervals in loops: a value defined late in one iteration and used early in the next wraps around the loop boundary, and the graph becomes a circular-arc graph, whose chromatic number can exceed its maximum overlap and whose coloring is NP-hard in general. Pipelined loops add modulo lifetimes. Tools then use heuristics, or unroll the kernel so lifetimes become intervals again, at the cost of a larger controller.

## Going deeper

Golumbic, "Algorithmic Graph Theory and Perfect Graphs" (2nd ed., 2004), chapter on interval graphs; De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 6.

lesson:
# Functional-unit binding by clique partitioning

Functional-unit binding decides which unit executes each operation. Tseng and Siewiorek cast it as clique partitioning of a compatibility graph: operations that could share a unit are adjacent, and each clique becomes one unit. The formulation also covers register binding and interconnect-aware binding, so it is the general framework behind HLS sharing decisions.

## The compatibility graph

Two operations are compatible when one unit can execute both: they are of a type the unit supports and they never need it at the same time. For single-cycle operations of one type, that means they are scheduled in different steps. Draw a vertex per operation and an edge per compatible pair. With seven multiplications in steps 6, 5, 4, 2, 6, 4 and 5, only pairs in the same step are incompatible: (m1, m5), (m2, m7) and (m3, m6). Of the 21 pairs, 18 are compatible, so the graph has 18 edges. A compatibility graph is the complement of a conflict graph; working with compatibility suits sharing problems because a set of operations that can all share one unit is exactly a clique in it.

## Cliques as units

A partition of the vertices into cliques is a binding: every clique is a set of mutually compatible operations, executed on one unit. The fewest cliques is the fewest units. For single-cycle operations of one type, the graph is complete multipartite, with one part per step, and the minimum clique cover equals the size of the largest part, the busiest step: one operation from each step can always be grouped together. With multiplications in steps 1, 4, 5, 1, 2 and 2, the busiest steps hold two, so two multipliers suffice, for example $\{m_1, m_5, m_2, m_3\}$ and $\{m_4, m_6\}$. Clique partitioning is NP-hard on general graphs, and Tseng and Siewiorek's heuristic repeatedly merges the pair of vertices with the most common neighbours, which tends to keep large cliques possible.

## Multicycle operations and weighted edges

With non-pipelined multicycle units, each operation occupies its unit for an interval $[s, s + L - 1]$, and two operations are compatible when their intervals do not overlap. The conflict graph is then an interval graph, and its complement, the compatibility graph, has a minimum clique cover equal to the maximum number of overlapping busy intervals, by perfection of interval graphs. Multiplications of latency 2 starting in steps 4, 4, 4 and 3 overlap in step 4 four at a time, so four multipliers are needed. Real binders go further and weight the edges by how much sharing costs: two operations reading the same registers can share a unit with no new multiplexer inputs, so their edge gets a high weight. Clique partitioning that maximizes total weight then minimizes interconnect as well as unit count.

## Going deeper

Tseng and Siewiorek, "Automated synthesis of data paths in digital systems" (IEEE TCAD, 1986); De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 6.

lesson:
# Interconnect and multiplexer cost

Sharing a functional unit or a register is not free: every distinct source that feeds a shared input port needs a multiplexer input. In FPGA designs these multiplexers can cost as much area as the units they enable sharing for, and they add delay to every path through the shared unit. Interconnect-aware binding is where HLS quality is often won or lost.

## Sources at a port

After binding, each input port of a unit receives operands from some set of registers or units across the steps in which it is used. A port fed from one source needs only a wire; a port fed from $k$ distinct sources needs a $k$-input multiplexer, whose select signal comes from the controller. Count the distinct sources, not the operations: if adder A1 executes $R_2 + R_5$, $R_1 + R_5$, $R_1 + R_3$ and $R_4 + R_1$, its left port reads $R_2$, $R_1$ and $R_4$, three distinct registers, so it needs a 3-input multiplexer, and its right port reads $R_5$, $R_3$ and $R_1$, also three. Register inputs are counted the same way: a register written by several units needs a multiplexer on its data input. The total multiplexer area grows with every additional distinct connection.

## Counting two-input multiplexer equivalents

A $k$-input multiplexer can be built from $k - 1$ two-input multiplexers, so a common cost measure is $\sum_{\text{ports}} (k_p - 1)$ over ports with $k_p \ge 1$ sources. For an adder executing $R_4 + R_6$, $R_3 + R_5$ and $R_2 + R_5$, the left port has 3 sources and the right port 2, so the cost is $(3 - 1) + (2 - 1) = 3$ two-input multiplexers. On FPGAs the real cost is in LUTs and depends on width: a 32-bit 4-input multiplexer costs 32 times a 1-bit one. Delay matters too: each level of multiplexing lengthens every path through the shared unit, which can cancel the clock-period gain the scheduler assumed. This is why HLS tools sometimes refuse to share small units such as adders, whose cost is close to that of the multiplexers that sharing them would need.

## Using commutativity

For commutative operations, the binder may swap operands, which changes which port each source feeds. The adder executing $R_3 + R_1$, $R_5 + R_2$, $R_1 + R_6$ and $R_3 + R_2$ costs $(3 - 1) + (3 - 1) = 4$ as written, because the left port reads $R_3, R_5, R_1$ and the right $R_1, R_2, R_6$. Swapping the third addition to $R_6 + R_1$ makes the left port read $R_3, R_5, R_6$ and the right $R_1, R_2$, for a cost of $2 + 1 = 3$. With $n$ commutative operations there are $2^n$ orientations, so binders use heuristics or fold the choice into a weighted bipartite matching between sources and ports. The same idea extends to choosing which register holds which value: binding values that feed the same port into the same register removes a multiplexer input entirely.

## Going deeper

De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 6, on interconnect and binding; Gajski, Dutt, Wu and Lin, "High-Level Synthesis" (1992), chapter on data-path synthesis.

lesson:
# The datapath and its FSM controller

The RTL an HLS tool emits has two halves. The datapath holds the functional units, registers and multiplexers chosen by allocation and binding. The controller is a finite-state machine that walks the schedule and, in every state, drives the multiplexer selects, register load enables and unit function selects. Knowing how one maps to the other lets a tool designer read generated RTL and predict where its critical paths and area go.

## Datapath and controller

The datapath computes and stores values: units, registers, multiplexers and the wires between them. The controller decides what the datapath does each cycle. In a statically scheduled design it is a Moore machine with one state per control step; in state $s$ it asserts the control word for step $s$: which source each multiplexer selects, which registers load, and which function each multi-function unit performs, such as add or subtract. A register that must capture a new value only in steps 2 and 5 has its load enable asserted in exactly those states, and holds its value otherwise. A loop whose body takes 4 steps becomes a cycle of 4 states with a conditional transition from the last state back to the first or out to the exit. The state register, next-state logic and output decoding are all controller logic.

## State count and encoding

A schedule of $S$ steps plus an idle state gives $S + 1$ states. Binary encoding needs $\lceil \log_2 (S + 1) \rceil$ flip-flops; one-hot encoding needs $S + 1$, one per state. A 16-step schedule with an idle state has 17 states, which binary encodes in 5 flip-flops and one-hot in 17. Binary saves flip-flops but every control signal must decode several state bits; one-hot makes each signal an OR of the few states that assert it, which is usually faster and is the common choice on FPGAs, where flip-flops are plentiful. Nested loops multiply control: each loop level adds its own states and counter, and HLS tools often generate a hierarchy of FSMs, one per loop or function, communicating through start and done signals.

## Where the controller shapes timing and area

Sharing moves cost from units into multiplexers and control: one adder shared by six additions needs input multiplexers and select signals decoded from the state. Heavy sharing adds multiplexer levels in front of every shared unit and lengthens its paths, which can force a slower clock. A large FSM with many states and high-fanout enable signals can itself become the critical path. Pipelined loops change the controller's shape: instead of one state per step of one iteration, the kernel repeats every II cycles, and stage-valid bits track which iterations are in flight during the prologue and epilogue. Variable-latency operations, such as a memory read that may stall, add wait states that loop until a valid or done signal arrives, so the schedule is no longer purely static.

## Going deeper

Gajski, Dutt, Wu and Lin, "High-Level Synthesis" (1992), chapter on control synthesis; De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 4.
